title: Impact of Road Density on Urban Population Growth

llm_response.content:
## 1. Identification Strategy  
Method: Two-Stage Least Squares (2SLS/IV).  
Why: Road density (x) is likely endogenous — cities that are already growing may lobby for more roads, creating reverse causality and omitted-variable bias. The 1947 highway plan (z) provides exogenous variation: it predetermined where major highways would be built long before the subsequent decades of urban growth captured in the data.  

Key IV assumptions  
1. Relevance: z must be correlated with x  
  Cov(z, x) ≠ 0 (testable via first-stage F-statistic).  
2. Exogeneity (exclusion restriction): z affects population growth (y) only through its impact on road density, conditional on controls (not directly testable, but argued historically because the 1947 plan was drafted before modern urban expansion).  
3. Monotonicity (no defiers): areas assigned more roads by the plan do not systematically build fewer roads.  

## 2. R Code
```r
# Required packages
required <- c("readr", "dplyr", "AER", "sandwich", "lmtest")
installed <- rownames(installed.packages())
for(p in required[!required %in% installed]) install.packages(p, repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")
lapply(required, library, character.only = TRUE)

# 1. Load data
data_path <- "experiments/exp_b/data/s77_data.csv"
df <- read_csv(data_path, show_col_types = FALSE)

# 2. Basic descriptives
cat("Observations:", nrow(df), "\n")
cat("Mean road density:", mean(df$x), "\n")
cat("Mean population growth:", mean(df$y), "\n\n")

# 3. OLS benchmark
ols <- lm(y ~ x + controls, data = df)
ols_robust <- coeftest(ols, vcov = vcovHC(ols, type = "HC1"))

cat("------- OLS (robust SE) -------\n")
print(ols_robust["x", ])

# 4. IV estimation (2SLS)
iv <- ivreg(y ~ x + controls | z + controls, data = df)
iv_robust <- coeftest(iv, vcov = vcovHC(iv, type = "HC1"))

cat("\n------- IV (2SLS, robust SE) -------\n")
print(iv_robust["x", ])

# 5. First-stage diagnostics
first_stage <- summary(iv$stage1, diagnostics = TRUE)
fs_F <- first_stage$diagnostics[["Weak instruments"]]["F"]
cat("\nFirst-stage F-statistic on instrument (rule-of-thumb >10):", round(fs_F, 2), "\n")

# 6. Over-identification is not applicable (single instrument), but
#    Wu-Hausman endogeneity test
hausman <- first_stage$diagnostics[["Wu-Hausman"]]["p-value"]
cat("Wu-Hausman endogeneity p-value:", round(hausman, 3), "\n")

# 7. Robustness check 1: add squared control
df <- df %>% mutate(controls_sq = controls^2)
iv_rb1 <- ivreg(y ~ x + controls + controls_sq | z + controls + controls_sq, data = df)
iv_rb1_robust <- coeftest(iv_rb1, vcov = vcovHC(iv_rb1, type = "HC1"))

cat("\nRobustness 1 (add controls^2) – x coefficient:\n")
print(iv_rb1_robust["x", ])

# 8. Robustness check 2: no controls
iv_rb2 <- ivreg(y ~ x | z, data = df)
iv_rb2_robust <- coeftest(iv_rb2, vcov = vcovHC(iv_rb2, type = "HC1"))

cat("\nRobustness 2 (no controls) – x coefficient:\n")
print(iv_rb2_robust["x", ])

# 9. Output concise result
coef_val  <- iv_robust["x", "Estimate"]
se_val    <- iv_robust["x", "Std. Error"]
t_val     <- iv_robust["x", "t value"]
p_val     <- iv_robust["x", "Pr(>|t|)"]

cat("\n======================================\n")
cat("Preferred IV estimate:\n")
cat("Effect of road density on population growth =", round(coef_val, 3),
    " (SE =", round(se_val, 3), ", t =", round(t_val, 2),
    ", p =", round(p_val, 3), ")\n")
cat("======================================\n")
```

## 3. Expected Findings  
Sign: Positive. Additional road density should ease commuting, attract firms, and raise residential construction, leading to faster population growth.  

Magnitude: Prior literature (e.g., Baum-Snow 2007) finds elasticities between 0.3 and 0.6. With variables standardised (as they appear to be mean-zero, SD≈1), I expect a coefficient ≈ 0.4–0.5; i.e., a 1-SD increase in road density raises population growth by roughly 0.4–0.5 SDs.

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: Use the 1947 highway plan as an instrument for road density.
_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: Increased road density leads to higher population growth in urban areas.
